rw: The annual fee is a yearly charge for keeping the card account open, separate from interest, and issuers often justify it with rewards, travel perks or other benefits that come with the card.

ww.Taxes on purchases made with the card: Sales taxes are collected by the seller at checkout on purchases, not by the card issuer, so they are never what the annual fee pays for.
ww.The price of items bought with the card: The price of purchases is what you owe the merchant through the card, billed separately, while the annual fee is a flat yearly charge for the account itself.
ww.Your interest charges on the card: Interest charges are billed on balances carried past the due date and are separate from the annual fee, which you owe even if you never carry a balance.

rw: Rewards are 2% x $2,000 = $40 a year, which is less than the $95 fee, so you lose $55 and the card does not pay for itself at that spending level.

ww.Yes: fees are free for the frequent user: Fees are not waived for frequent users; an annual fee is charged to the account regardless of how much you spend, unless the issuer specifically offers a waiver.
ww.It cannot be calculated from the data: The answer can be calculated: the spending, reward rate and fee are all given, and multiplying 2% by $2,000 and comparing to $95 settles it.
ww.Yes: $40 is more than the $95 fee: This is wrong because $40 is smaller than $95, not larger; the rewards earn $40 against a $95 fee, leaving a net loss of $55 per year.

rw: With equal balances, the 22% card accrues the most interest each month, so paying it down first (the avalanche method) saves the most money overall.

ww.The 15% card: The 15% card costs the least in interest, so paying extra on it saves the least; extra payments should go to the highest rate instead.
ww.The 18% card: The 18% card is in the middle, so extra payments there save more than on the 15% card but less than on the 22% card.
ww.All equally: Cards with different APRs do not cost the same in interest, so paying them down equally wastes savings; with equal balances, the highest rate costs the most.

rw: Credit repair means disputing real errors on your reports and building better habits, like on-time payments and low balances, which gradually improves your credit score over time.

ww.Paying a company to guarantee a perfect: No company can legally guarantee a perfect score, and credit repair firms that promise this regardless of your history are making a common deceptive claim.
ww.Erasing true negative information on req: True and accurate negative information, such as real late payments, generally stays on a report for years, and a firm cannot lawfully force its removal on request.
ww.Hiding your credit report from lenders a: Credit reports cannot be hidden from lenders who have a permissible purpose, and trying to conceal them does not improve a score or history at all.

rw: A deductible is the set amount you pay yourself each plan year for covered care before the insurer begins sharing costs through coinsurance or paying benefits.

ww.The most the plan pays, in a year, for a: That describes an out-of-pocket maximum, the most you pay in a year, after which the plan covers covered care; a deductible is only the first portion you pay.
ww.The monthly premium that you pay to the: The monthly premium is the regular payment that keeps coverage active, and you owe it whether or not you use care; the deductible is separate.
ww.A tax on medical care that patients pay: A deductible is not a tax; it is a cost-sharing term in the insurance contract, and the money goes to the providers of your care, not to the government.

rw: After the deductible is met, the patient pays 20% coinsurance: 0.20 x $1,000 = $200, and the insurer pays the remaining $800 of the bill.

ww.$1,000: The $1,000 bill is below the $1,500 deductible only if the deductible is unmet; the question says it is already met, so coinsurance applies instead of the full bill.
ww.$1,500: The $1,500 deductible is already paid and does not apply again, and a $1,000 bill cannot cost the patient more than the bill itself.
ww.$800: $800 is the insurer's 80% share of the bill; the patient owes the other 20%, so 0.20 x $1,000 = $200 is the patient's share, not $800.

rw: The insurer pays the loss minus the deductible: $3,000 - $500 = $2,500, which is within the $12,000 coverage limit, so the full remainder is covered.

ww.$3,000: $3,000 would be paid only with no deductible; the $500 deductible comes out first, so the insurer pays $2,500 and the renter bears $500.
ww.$500: $500 is the deductible, the amount the renter pays, not what the insurer pays; the insurer covers the remaining $2,500 of the loss.
ww.$12,000: $12,000 is the policy's coverage limit, the maximum payout, not the amount paid; the insurer pays only the actual loss less the deductible.

rw: An exclusion lists causes of loss or property the policy does not cover, such as floods in many homeowners policies, so the insurer pays nothing for them.

ww.A discount on the cost of the policy: A discount lowers the price of the policy, but an exclusion does the opposite kind of job: it narrows what is covered and does not reduce premiums.
ww.A bonus payment from the insurance firm: A bonus payment from the insurer is not an exclusion; exclusions limit coverage and never add money, so they cannot be a payout of any kind.
ww.A refund of premium at the end of term: A refund of premium at the end of a term is a different feature; an exclusion limits what the insurer will pay on a claim and refunds nothing.

rw: Reading shows which events, limits, deductibles and exclusions apply, so you know what is covered before you file a claim or decide to buy more coverage.

ww.To make claims easier without reading it: Claims are not easier if you skip reading the policy; not knowing the terms often causes denied claims and unpleasant surprises when you need coverage.
ww.Because it is entertaining to read at ho: Policies are dense legal documents that few people enjoy, and entertainment is not the reason to read them; the real reason is protecting yourself.
ww.To avoid paying premiums for the policy: You still owe premiums to keep coverage in force; reading the policy does not remove them, though it may help you spot discounts or unneeded coverage.

rw: Skipping insurance to save $300 a month left the person exposed to a $40,000 bill; insurance exists to transfer large, unlikely losses and protect finances.

ww.Buying too much insurance in this case: The person bought no insurance, so buying too much is not the error; the problem was too little protection against a large and unpredictable cost.
ww.Having a low deductible on the plan: The person had no plan at all, so a low deductible was not the issue; a lower deductible would actually have reduced the out-of-pocket cost.
ww.Saving too much money for the future: Saving money is generally good, and the person did not save too much; the error was ignoring a major risk that savings of $300 a month could not cover.

rw: A claim is the formal request a policyholder files with the insurer asking for payment or services after a covered loss such as an accident, theft or illness.

ww.A monthly bill that the insurer sends to: A monthly bill sent to the policyholder is a premium notice; a claim goes the other way, from the policyholder to the insurer, asking for payment.
ww.A tax return that you file with the IRS: A tax return is filed with the IRS to report income and has nothing to do with insurance; a claim is made to an insurer after a loss.
ww.A refund of a deductible, paid by the in: A refund of a deductible is not what a claim is; a claim is the request itself, and the deductible is normally subtracted from any payout instead.

rw: Safety comes first: check yourself and others for injuries and call 911 if anyone is hurt or the road is blocked, then exchange information and document the scene.

ww.Argue about fault with the other driver: Arguing about fault at the scene wastes time, can escalate, and is not the insurers' job; stay calm, trade information, and let the insurers decide fault.
ww.Post about it online before you call any: Posting online first can hurt your claim, since statements may be used against you, and calling for help for anyone injured is more urgent than posting.
ww.Leave the scene of the accident before h: Leaving the scene before help arrives can be hit-and-run in many states, a crime that can bring fines or jail and also jeopardize your insurance coverage.

rw: Fraud is intentional deception to gain money or property, such as identity theft, false insurance claims or fake investment schemes, and it is a crime.

ww.A discount on the price of goods: A discount lowers a price and involves no deception, so it is not fraud; fraud is dishonesty intended to take money or property unfairly from someone.
ww.A fair trade between two parties: A fair trade is an honest exchange where both parties understand and agree, which is the opposite of fraud, where one side is deliberately misled.
ww.A legal contract signed by both sides: A legal contract signed by both sides is a valid agreement, not fraud, though a contract obtained through lies or false statements can be fraudulent.

rw: A data breach happens when unauthorized people gain access to personal or financial data, such as card numbers or Social Security numbers, often through hacking.

ww.A bank holiday when all the branches are: A bank holiday is a day when branches are closed and has nothing to do with data security; a breach is a security failure, not a closure.
ww.A system update that fixes bugs in a com: A system update that fixes bugs is routine maintenance and in fact helps prevent breaches; it is not an unauthorized intrusion into your data.
ww.A password change that you make on a web: Changing your own password is a protective step you take, not an attack; a breach is when someone else gets in without permission.

rw: A fraud alert or credit freeze makes it harder for thieves to open new accounts in your name, and monitoring accounts helps you catch misuse early.

ww.Share your information widely with other: Sharing your information widely online gives criminals more material for identity theft, which is the opposite of protecting your credit after a breach.
ww.Close all of your bank accounts at rando: Closing every bank account at random is disruptive and unnecessary; it does not stop misuse of exposed data and can hurt your credit and finances.
ww.Do nothing and hope that the thieves los: Doing nothing leaves exposed data open to misuse, and thieves do not lose interest; acting quickly is the main defense against identity theft.

rw: A credit freeze restricts access to your credit report so lenders cannot approve new accounts in your name, which stops most identity thieves from opening credit.

ww.A tax that is charged on every credit ca: A tax charged on credit accounts has no relation to a freeze; a credit freeze is a free consumer protection, not a levy on cards or accounts.
ww.A fee for freezing assets, charged by th: Credit freezes are free under federal law since 2018, so there is no bank fee, and a freeze blocks credit access instead of freezing your assets.
ww.A loan that the bank gives you after you: A freeze does not produce a loan; it is a protective lock on your credit file, which you can lift temporarily when you apply for credit yourself.

rw: Life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries, replacing income and covering debts, funeral costs and living expenses for the family the insured leaves behind.

ww.To pay for retirement when the insured p: Retirement income is the purpose of annuities and retirement accounts, while life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries rather than funding the insured's old age.
ww.To save for a vacation that the family p: Vacations are paid for with savings, not life insurance; the policy pays out only on death and is not a savings plan for planned trips.
ww.To lower taxes that the family owes the: Life insurance does not reduce the taxes a family owes; its purpose is replacing income and covering costs, though death benefits are often received tax free.

rw: With no dependents and few debts, nobody relies on the person's income, so only final expenses like funeral costs need covering and a large policy is unnecessary.

ww.Ten times income always, whatever their: A fixed multiple of income is a rule of thumb that suits people with dependents; for a single person with no dependents it would waste premium money.
ww.A policy for every pet that they own at: Pets are not insured by life insurance, which pays for the death of a person, and a pet policy would not address this person's actual needs.
ww.The most expensive policy that they can: The most expensive policy is not needed when no one relies on the income; buying more coverage than your situation requires wastes money on premiums.

rw: Interviews let employers assess skills, attitude and fit for the job and the team, going beyond the written résumé to judge how a person would perform.

ww.To avoid hiring anyone for the open posi: Employers interview because they want to hire someone for an open position, so avoiding hiring would defeat the point of spending time and money on the process.
ww.To tell the candidate the company's priv: Employers do not share confidential business secrets with candidates, who have not been hired, and sharing them could damage the company.
ww.To test the candidate's typing speed onl: Typing speed may be one part of some jobs, but interviews assess many skills and traits, like communication, experience and fit, not typing alone.

rw: She earns $11 x 12 hours = $132 per week, and 4 weeks x $132 = $528 before taxes are withheld from her paycheck.

ww.$132: $132 is one week of pay: $11 x 12 hours = $132; the question asks about a 4-week month, so that weekly amount must be multiplied by 4.
ww.$48: $48 is only the number of hours worked in the month (12 x 4), not the pay; pay is hours multiplied by the $11 hourly wage.
ww.$5,280: $5,280 is far too high, arising from multiplying by 10 somewhere; the correct calculation is $11 x 12 x 4 = $528.

rw: A pay stub shows hours, pay rate, gross pay and deductions, so reviewing it lets workers catch payroll mistakes and underpayments before they become bigger problems.

ww.To avoid keeping any records of pay at a: Workers should keep pay records for tax time, loan applications and disputes, so avoiding records would be a poor financial habit and could cause problems later.
ww.To pay their employer for the right to s: Workers never pay an employer to see their pay stub; employers must provide pay information, and charging for it would not be an ordinary practice.
ww.To lower their tax rate by changing the: Changing numbers on a pay stub is falsification, not tax planning; tax rates are set by law and withholding is changed through proper forms like the W-4.

rw: Healthcare is a need people cannot skip in a downturn, so nurses see steady demand and hiring, which makes the job relatively recession resistant.

ww.A concert ticket reseller who sells tick: Ticket resale depends on discretionary entertainment spending, which falls sharply in a recession, so resellers face unstable demand and unstable income.
ww.A vacation planner for luxury trips for: Luxury trip planning relies on wealthy customers' discretionary travel, which is cut back in a recession, making that job less secure than essential work.
ww.A luxury yacht salesperson who works on: Yacht sales depend on luxury spending that collapses in recessions, and commission pay makes income even more unstable when buyers disappear.

rw: On commission only, a worker is paid a percentage of sales made and earns nothing without sales, so income can be high in good months and low in bad ones.

ww.You receive the same pay every single we: Getting the same pay every week describes a fixed salary or steady hourly pay, whereas commission only pay rises and falls with the sales you make.
ww.You receive a fixed bonus each pay perio: A fixed bonus each pay period is guaranteed money, whereas commission depends on sales results; the two are different forms of pay.
ww.You are paid by the hour of work you do: Hourly workers are paid for time worked, whereas commission only workers are paid for sales results, no matter how many hours they spend.

rw: Clear communication, spoken and written, helps with teamwork, customer service and avoiding mistakes, which is why employers rank it near the top in nearly every field.

ww.Ignoring deadlines: Ignoring deadlines hurts teams and projects, and employers see it as unreliability, so it is the opposite of a skill employers value.
ww.Avoiding teamwork: Employers want people who can collaborate, so avoiding teamwork is a weakness in nearly every workplace rather than a skill.
ww.Interrupting others: Interrupting others shows poor listening and respect, and it harms working relationships, so employers do not value it as a skill.

rw: The commute costs $200 x 12 = $2,400 per year, so net gain is $3,000 - $2,400 = $600 per year, much smaller than the raise suggests.

ww.$2,400: $2,400 is the raise minus $600; the commute cost is $200 x 12 = $2,400 per year, so $2,400 is the cost, not the net gain.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 is the raise before subtracting the commute cost; ignoring the $2,400 a year in commuting expenses overstates her real gain.
ww.$5,400: $5,400 adds the commute cost to the raise instead of subtracting it ($3,000 + $2,400); higher costs reduce her gain rather than increase it.

rw: A cost-of-living adjustment raises pay, often tied to inflation measures, so a worker's income keeps up with rising prices and purchasing power stays stable.

ww.A tax on wages that workers pay to the s: A tax on wages is a payroll or income tax, which is unrelated; a cost-of-living adjustment is an increase to pay, not a levy.
ww.A fee for moving to a new city for a dif: Moving fees or relocation assistance relate to changing cities, while a cost-of-living adjustment is a raise in pay for the same job as prices change.
ww.A reduction in pay that the employer mak: A pay cut would be the reverse of a cost-of-living adjustment, which increases pay to offset inflation and does not reduce what the worker earns.

rw: Her pay is flat while prices rise 4% yearly, so the same $30,000 buys fewer goods each year and her real buying power falls over time.

ww.It stays the same: With prices up 4% a year and pay frozen at $30,000, each dollar buys less, so buying power cannot stay the same.
ww.It rises over time: Buying power would rise only if pay grew faster than prices; with pay flat and prices climbing 4%, her purchasing power shrinks instead.
ww.It doubles each year: Prices rise 4% a year, not 100%, so buying power does not double; it declines slowly as inflation erodes the value of unchanged pay.

rw: Job training builds skills and knowledge that make workers more productive, which can lead to raises, promotions and better job opportunities over a career.

ww.Lowering your pay on purpose, so the emp: Training does not lower pay on purpose; employers invest in training to build skills that make workers more productive and valuable to the company.
ww.Avoiding a career in the job market for: Training prepares workers for the job market and does not take them out of it; it helps careers rather than avoiding them.
ww.Reducing your skills so that employers p: Training adds to skills, so it cannot reduce them, and employers pay more, not less, for workers with stronger and more current skills.

rw: Meeting deadlines shows reliability and keeps projects on schedule, which builds trust with managers and coworkers and supports career advancement.

ww.It is optional for all jobs, as deadline: Deadlines are not optional hints; missing them delays other people's work and costs trust, and employers expect workers to deliver on time.
ww.It lowers pay for everyone in the office: Meeting deadlines does not lower pay for everyone; if anything, missing them harms the company's results and can limit raises and promotions.
ww.It has no effect on others in the team o: Work is connected, so late work affects teammates who depend on it; deadlines matter because delays spread to others and to the whole project.

rw: Unit price, such as cost per ounce or per item, puts different package sizes on equal footing, so you can see which product truly costs less.

ww.Compare only the total price: Total price alone is misleading when sizes differ, since a larger package costs more but may hold much more; you need price per unit to compare fairly.
ww.Choose the smaller package always: The smaller package is not always cheaper per unit, since larger packages often have a lower unit price; always choosing small can cost more per ounce.
ww.Choose the bigger package always: Bigger is not always cheaper per unit, and it may spoil or go unused; picking size without comparing unit prices can waste money.

rw: Repair costs $120 for 1 more year, or $120 per year, while a new phone costs $400 / 3 years = about $133 per year, so repair is cheaper.

ww.Neither has any cost: Both options have costs, since repair costs $120 and a new phone costs $400; saying neither has any cost ignores the money involved.
ww.They cost exactly the same: The costs are not equal: repair is $120 per year and the new phone is about $133 per year ($400 / 3), so repair is a bit cheaper.
ww.New phone at $400 per year: The new phone is $400 / 3 years, which is about $133 per year of use, not $400 per year, and that is higher than the $120 repair.

rw: A subscription trap is a free trial that automatically becomes a paid plan with recurring charges unless you cancel before it ends, often with hard-to-find cancellation steps.

ww.A discount that never ends for those who: A discount that never ends is a benefit, not a trap; a subscription trap works against you by billing you after you forget to cancel a trial.
ww.A tax credit given to those who sign up: Tax credits come from the government and are not offered by subscriptions; a subscription trap is a marketing tactic that bills you for a plan.
ww.A permanent refund of all money paid to: A permanent refund is the opposite of a trap; in a subscription trap the company keeps charging you and makes money back difficult to get.

rw: Conspicuous consumption means buying goods or services mainly to display wealth or status to others, such as luxury cars or designer labels, rather than for need.

ww.Saving all income that you earn: Saving all your income is the opposite of consumption; conspicuous consumption involves spending, especially to impress others, not holding onto money.
ww.Buying only needs like food and shelter: Buying only needs like food and shelter is basic necessary spending, not a display of status, so it does not fit conspicuous consumption.
ww.Buying used items at a thrift store: Buying used items at a thrift store is thrifty and does not aim to display status, so it is the opposite of conspicuous consumption.

rw: Cost per wear is the price divided by the wears: $120 / 200 = $0.60, which shows how durable items used often can be cheap in the long run.

ww.$60.00: $60 is wrong by a factor of 100; dividing $120 by 200 wears gives far less than $60, because the cost is spread across many wears.
ww.$6.00: $6.00 is off by a factor of ten; $120 / 200 = $0.60, since 200 wears is a large number and spreads the price thin.
ww.$1.20: $1.20 would be $120 / 100 wears; with 200 wears the correct figure is half of that, $0.60 per wear.

rw: Small, cheap items near the register tempt shoppers into impulse purchases while waiting, adding to the sale at little perceived cost to the shopper.

ww.To hide products from shoplifters: Stores guard against shoplifting with cameras and staff placement, but placing small items at checkout is a sales tactic that targets shoppers waiting in line.
ww.To lower prices on small goods: Impulse items near checkout are usually priced normally or higher, not lowered; the placement aims to raise sales, not to cut prices on small goods.
ww.To reduce sales of small goods: Stores want sales, so reducing sales of small goods would defeat the purpose; checkout placement is meant to increase them.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up, so spending $50 on a game means losing the chance to save or spend it elsewhere.

ww.Nothing, because money is unlimited for: Money is limited, so spending $50 always means giving up something else; saying the opportunity cost is nothing ignores scarcity, which is basic to economics.
ww.The price of the game only, not what you: Price is the monetary cost, but opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up, so naming only the price misses the point.
ww.The sales tax only, not the price of the: Sales tax is part of the monetary cost, but opportunity cost is the value of the next best use of the money, not tax alone.

rw: 30% of $4,000 = 0.30 x $4,000 = $1,200, which is the most the household should spend on housing under the rule.

ww.$12,000: $12,000 is ten times too big, likely from a decimal error; 30% of $4,000 is $1,200, since 30% is less than a third of income.
ww.$120: $120 is only 3% of $4,000, a decimal slip; 30% means 0.30 x $4,000 = $1,200 for the housing limit.

rw: A refund policy spells out whether you can return items, the time limit, the condition required and whether you get cash, store credit or an exchange.

ww.A required discount that a store gives t: Stores are not required to give discounts; a refund policy states conditions for returns, and what a store offers beyond the law is up to its own rules.
ww.A tax on returns that a store adds to th: A refund policy is not a tax; it explains whether and when you can return items, and does not add charges to the price of items.
ww.A product's warranty only, covering repa: A warranty covers repair or replacement for defects, while a refund policy is about returns for money back, so the two are different protections.

rw: Needs are essentials like food, housing, utilities and transportation to work, which you must pay for to live and earn income, so they form the needs category.

ww.Spending on luxury items such as jewelry: Luxury items like jewelry and boats are wants, not needs, so they belong in a wants category of a budget and not a needs category.
ww.Spending on entertainment such as movies: Entertainment such as movies and video games is a want, since you can live without it; it belongs in the wants part of a budget.
ww.Spending on gifts for friends only, whic: Gifts are generally wants, but needs-based categories cover essentials like food and housing, so gifts alone do not describe the category.

rw: Each lunch costs $9 - $3 = $6 extra, so 20 lunches cost an extra $6 x 20 = $120 per month, which shows how small habits add up.

ww.$12: $12 is only the part of one lunch that is extra ($9 - $3 = $6) doubled by mistake; the full amount comes from multiplying by 20 lunches.
ww.$180: $180 is 20 lunches at $9 each, the total cost of buying; the extra over making lunch at home is $6 per lunch, not $9.
ww.$60: $60 is the cost of making 20 lunches at home ($3 x 20); the question asks for the extra cost of buying, which is $6 x 20 = $120.

rw: With cash envelopes, you can see money shrinking, and when an envelope is empty you stop spending, so the physical limit makes overspending easy to see.

ww.Envelopes remove the need for a plan or: Envelopes require a plan, since you must decide how much goes in each category beforehand, so they support budgeting instead of replacing it.
ww.Cash earns interest while it sits in an: Cash in an envelope earns no interest at all, unlike money in a savings account, so interest is not a reason to use envelopes.
ww.Envelopes build credit with the bank eve: Paying in cash does not report anything to credit bureaus, so envelopes do not build credit; only borrowing and repayment history builds credit.

rw: Buying only planned items keeps sales from causing overspending, so you save on things you needed and avoid impulse buys that break your budget.

ww.Buy two of every item that is marked dow: Buying two of everything marked down is wasteful, since a discount only saves money on things you would actually use or buy anyway.
ww.Buy anything marked down, whether or not: Buying anything marked down whether or not you need it spends money you did not plan to, and a sale price is still money spent.
ww.Spend your whole paycheck on sale items: Spending a whole paycheck on sale items ignores bills and savings, so it destroys a budget; a sale is never a reason to abandon a plan.

rw: As not-for-profit, member-owned institutions, credit unions often offer higher savings rates, lower loan rates and fewer fees than many for-profit banks.

ww.They always pay no interest, as credit u: Credit unions usually pay interest on savings, often higher than banks, and being member-owned does not mean they pay none.
ww.They never insure deposits of any member: Credit unions are federally insured by the NCUA, up to $250,000 per depositor, much like FDIC insurance at banks, so deposits are protected.
ww.They are not regulated by any government: Credit unions are regulated by government agencies such as the NCUA, which supervises federal credit unions and insures member deposits.

rw: Dividing the goal by the time: $6,000 / 24 months = $250 per month, ignoring interest, which would reach the down payment exactly.

ww.$144: $144 times 24 months is only $3,456, short of $6,000; you must divide the goal by the number of months to find the monthly saving.
ww.$2,500: $2,500 per month is far too high and would total $60,000 over 24 months; the goal of $6,000 spread over 24 months is much smaller.
ww.$25: $25 a month for 24 months would save only $600, one tenth of the $6,000 needed, so it is a decimal error.

rw: Cash at home can be stolen, lost or destroyed in a fire, and it earns no interest, while insured bank accounts protect and grow your money.

ww.It earns the highest interest of any acc: Cash at home earns no interest at all; accounts like high-yield savings or CDs pay more, so cash is not the highest-earning option.
ww.It grows automatically while it stays at: Cash does not grow by itself, and inflation slowly reduces its buying power, whereas interest-bearing accounts add earnings automatically over time.
ww.It is illegal to keep money at home in t: Keeping cash at home is perfectly legal in the United States; the reasons to avoid it are risk of loss and missed interest, not the law.

rw: A milestone is a checkpoint along the way, such as reaching $500 of a $5,000 goal, which keeps you motivated and shows progress.

ww.A bank fee for the savings account you k: A bank fee is a cost charged by a bank, not a goal marker; a milestone is a progress point on the way to a bigger target.
ww.A tax on savings that you pay each year: Taxes on savings are a separate matter; a savings milestone is just a checkpoint, such as saving the first $1,000, that tracks progress.
ww.A type of loan that you take out to buy: A loan is borrowed money, but a savings milestone marks progress in saving your own money, so the two concepts are not the same.

rw: Interest is 4% x $2,500 = $100, and the balance is $2,500 + $100 = $2,600 after one year, since APY already includes compounding.

ww.$2,540: $2,540 would be 1.6% interest; 4% of $2,500 is $100, not $40, so the balance after one year is larger than this figure.
ww.$2,504: $2,504 adds only $4, which is 0.16% interest; the 4% rate gives $100 of interest on $2,500, so the balance is $2,600.
ww.$3,500: $3,500 would add $1,000, equal to 40% interest; 4% of $2,500 is only $100, so the balance is $2,600.

rw: A liquid account lets you get money quickly without penalty or loss of value, like a savings or checking account, which suits emergency funds.

ww.The money is invested in land and homes: Money invested in land or homes is hard to sell fast, so it is illiquid, which is the opposite of the meaning of liquid.
ww.The money is spent already on bills: Money already spent on bills is gone and not an account feature; liquidity describes how easily savings can be turned into cash.
ww.The money is locked for many years: Money locked for many years is illiquid, as with a long-term CD or retirement account, which is the opposite of liquid.

rw: The 50/30/20 guideline puts 50% of after-tax income toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings or paying down debt, giving a simple budget structure.

ww.Fifty days saving for thirty days spendi: The guideline is about percentages of income, not days; it does not involve days of saving, spending or rest in any way.
ww.Fifty percent borrowed, thirty percent l: The rule has nothing to do with borrowing, lending or giving away money; it divides after-tax income among needs, wants and savings or debt.
ww.Half to wants, thirty percent to needs a: The percentages are reversed and misassigned here: 50% goes to needs and 30% to wants, with 20% to savings or debt, not to taxes.

rw: Needs get 50% of income: 0.50 x $3,000 = $1,500 a month, covering essentials like rent, food, utilities and transportation.

ww.$600: $600 is 20% of $3,000, the savings and debt share; the needs share under the rule is 50%.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 is the entire monthly income; needs get only 50% of it under 50/30/20, with the rest going to wants and savings or debt.
ww.$900: $900 is 30% of $3,000, the share for wants; needs receive 50%, which is a larger share.

rw: APY includes compounding, so it shows what a deposit will really earn in a year and lets you compare savings accounts and CDs fairly.

ww.Calculating taxes owed on the income you: Taxes owed on income are figured using tax rates and brackets, not APY, which is a measure of the yield earned on deposit accounts.
ww.Measuring inflation and the rise in pric: Inflation is tracked with price indexes such as the CPI, not APY, which measures account earnings, not the rise in prices.
ww.Comparing loan fees charged by different: Loan costs are compared using APR and fees; APY is for deposit accounts and tells you what you earn, not what you pay.

rw: A small starter emergency fund, such as $500 to $1,000, gives a cushion for surprises and is realistic and achievable for beginners.

ww.A luxury item with a large price: A large luxury purchase is a want, and starting with it delays building a safety net for emergencies, so it is not a good first goal.
ww.A complicated investment plan: A complicated investment plan is premature without an emergency fund, and it may add risk that a beginner does not yet need or understand.
ww.No goal at all for the time being: Having no goal makes saving harder, since goals give direction and motivation; a simple, specific first goal helps build the habit.

rw: In a Roth IRA you contribute after-tax money, and earnings grow tax free with qualified withdrawals also tax free in retirement, which suits young savers with decades to grow.

ww.It guarantees stock gains every year, wh: Roth IRA investments can lose value, as nothing guarantees stock gains each year; the account is a tax advantage, not a promise of returns.
ww.It has no contribution limits, so anyone: Roth IRAs have annual contribution limits set by the IRS and income limits for eligibility, so not everyone can contribute any amount.
ww.It must be spent within a year of being: A Roth IRA has no deadline to spend the money within a year; it is a long-term retirement account that is meant to stay invested.

rw: Blue chip stocks come from large, well-established, financially sound companies with a long record of reliable earnings, and many pay dividends.

ww.A stock priced under a dollar per share: Penny stocks sell for under a dollar and are often risky; blue chips are the opposite, being large, stable, well-known companies.
ww.A stock of a new startup with little his: A new startup with little history is a riskier, unproven stock; blue chip stocks come from firms with long records of stable earnings.
ww.A stock that pays no dividends to anyone: Many blue chips actually pay regular dividends, so having no dividends does not define them; what defines them is size and stability.

rw: After the fall the value is $800, and a 25% rise adds 0.25 x $800 = $200, bringing it back to $1,000, which shows losses and gains are not symmetric.

ww.$1,025: $1,025 is wrong because the 25% rise applies to $800, not $1,000; 25% of $800 is $200, so the value is $1,000.
ww.$800: $800 is the value after the fall, before the rise; the 25% rise adds $200, so the value after the rise is $1,000.
ww.$1,250: $1,250 would result from a 25% rise on $1,000, but the rise applies to the lower $800 value, giving $800 x 1.25 = $1,000.

rw: Volatility measures how widely and quickly prices swing up and down; higher volatility means bigger changes and more risk and uncertainty for investors.

ww.A fee charged by brokers on each trade y: Fees charged by brokers are trading costs or commissions, which are unrelated to price swings that volatility describes.
ww.A guarantee of steady prices for the nex: Volatility is the opposite of steady prices; no market can guarantee stable prices, and volatile markets move unpredictably.
ww.A tax on gains that investors pay each y: A tax on gains is capital gains tax, which is unrelated; volatility describes how much prices change, not what is owed on profits.

rw: Social media tips can be mistaken, made by people with something to gain, or part of pump and dump scams, so relying on them is risky.

ww.Tips always lead to profit for every inv: Tips do not always lead to profit; many lose money because they are late, wrong or promoted by people who profit when others buy.
ww.Tips are always guaranteed by regulators: Social media tips are not guaranteed by regulators, who do not vet random posts; the SEC warns that many tips are scams or hype.
ww.Tips remove all risk for the investor wh: Every investment carries risk, and no tip removes it; acting on unverified advice can actually increase the chance of losing money.

rw: The fee is 0.05% x $10,000 = $5 per year, which is very low and shows why low-cost index funds are popular with investors.

ww.About $50 per year in fees: $50 would be 0.5% of $10,000; the fund's 0.05% fee is ten times smaller, so the correct figure is lower than this.
ww.About $500 per year in fees: $500 would be a 5% expense ratio, which is 100 times the 0.05% given, so it is far too high.
ww.No fees at all each year: An expense ratio is an annual fee charged by the fund, so there are fees every year, even when small, such as $5 on $10,000.

rw: Municipal bonds are issued by states, cities and other local governments to fund projects like schools and roads, and interest is often exempt from federal tax.

ww.A loan from a bank to a single private p: A bank loan to a private person is a personal loan, not a municipal bond; municipal bonds are issued by governments, not by lenders to individuals.
ww.A savings account at a city bank for res: A savings account at a city bank is a deposit product, not a bond; a municipal bond is a debt security issued by a government.
ww.A stock of a city's shops and malls toda: A municipal bond is debt, not equity, so it is not a stock; stocks represent ownership of companies, not loans to governments.

rw: The 60-year-old has less time before needing the money, so a big stock market drop may not recover in time; this raises the risk of loss.

ww.The 30-year-old, with more time to recov: The 30-year-old has decades to recover from market drops, so a large temporary loss matters less than for someone close to needing the money.
ww.Neither, because risk is identical at an: Risk is not identical at any age, since time horizon matters; those near retirement face more risk from a drop because they cannot wait to recover.
ww.Neither, because stocks never fall in va: Stocks can and do fall in value, sometimes sharply, as in 2008, so claiming they never fall is false and ignores real market history.

rw: A limit order sets the price you will accept: a buy at that price or lower, or a sale at that price or higher, giving price control but no guarantee of execution.

ww.An order at any price right now, carried: An order filled at any price right now is a market order; a limit order sets a price condition and may not be filled immediately.
ww.An order to cancel a trade that you plac: Canceling a trade is done with a cancel request; a limit order is an instruction to buy or sell at a set price.
ww.An order to hold a stock for the long te: Holding for the long term is an investment strategy, not an order type; a limit order simply sets the price at which you will trade.

rw: Fees come out of returns every time, and the lost money also stops compounding, so over decades high fees can cost thousands of dollars.

ww.They raise returns, since brokers work h: Higher fees reduce returns; brokers working harder does not raise your returns, and fees are a cost that comes directly out of your investment gains.
ww.They are tax free for all investors in a: Trading fees are costs that reduce returns, and fees are not tax free; they may even limit some tax benefits, so this claim is wrong.
ww.They remove risk from your whole portfol: Fees cannot remove risk; they add a cost, and a portfolio still carries market risk regardless of the fees you pay.

rw: Prime borrowers have strong credit histories and high scores and get the best rates, while subprime borrowers have weaker credit and pay higher rates.

ww.Prime borrowers have no income and subpr: Both prime and subprime borrowers have incomes; the classification depends on credit history and scores, not on having no income versus large incomes.
ww.Subprime borrowers pay lower rates, as l: Subprime borrowers pay higher rates, not lower, because lenders charge more to offset the greater risk of default from weaker credit records.
ww.There is no difference between prime and: There is a clear difference, since lenders classify borrowers by credit risk and price loans accordingly, so prime and subprime borrowers get different terms.

rw: The 5-year loan has a lower payment but you owe interest for 60 months instead of 36, so total interest is higher; this is the trade-off.

ww.A longer loan has no interest at all to: A longer loan still charges interest every month; saying it has none at all is false, and interest typically adds up to more over the extra time.
ww.A longer loan costs less interest overal: A longer loan costs more interest overall, not less, because the balance stays outstanding for more months, even though each monthly payment is smaller.
ww.The loans cost exactly the same in inter: The loans do not cost the same, since a longer term means more months of interest; the payment is lower but the total paid is higher.

rw: Length of credit history is a scoring factor, so keeping old accounts open lengthens your average account age and can help your score.

ww.Old accounts always cost money to keep o: Old accounts without annual fees cost nothing to keep, and keeping them open helps your score; closing them may even hurt it.
ww.They prevent you from borrowing any mone: Open old accounts do not stop you from borrowing; they actually add to your available credit and can make borrowing easier.
ww.They reduce your score always, by a lot: Keeping accounts open generally helps your score; closing them can reduce available credit and average account age, so the claim is wrong.

rw: APR is the annual percentage rate, expressing the yearly cost of a loan including interest and certain fees, so you can compare loans fairly.

ww.The loan length in months or years that: Loan length is the term, such as 60 months, whereas APR is an annual rate that includes the cost of borrowing, not how long the loan lasts.
ww.The monthly payment that you make to the: The monthly payment is a dollar amount; APR is a yearly percentage rate and not a payment amount.
ww.The loan amount that you borrow from the: The amount borrowed is the principal; APR is a percentage describing the yearly cost of borrowing, not the size of the loan.

rw: Cash advances usually carry an upfront fee, a higher interest rate than purchases, and interest that starts immediately with no grace period.

ww.It is free of charge and carries no cost: Cash advances are not free; issuers charge fees and high rates, so saying there is no cost to the borrower is false.
ww.It has no interest and no fees of any ki: Cash advances carry both interest and fees, so it is wrong to say there is neither; they are one of the most expensive ways to borrow.
ww.It builds credit quickly, as the lender: Lenders do not give credit for taking a cash advance, and it can signal financial stress and raise utilization, so it does not build credit.

rw: FICO and VantageScore both run from 300 to 850, with higher scores showing lower risk and better chances of getting loans at good rates.

ww.1 to 5: A 1 to 5 range is not used for credit scores; common scoring models such as FICO and VantageScore use a much wider numerical range.
ww.0 to 10: A 0 to 10 range is not used for credit scores; the commonly used models have three-digit numbers, not a single-digit scale.
ww.1000 to 5000: A range of 1000 to 5000 is not a common credit score range; the main models use 300 to 850 instead.

rw: A down payment is the part of the price paid up front, which lowers the amount borrowed and shows the lender the buyer has a stake in the purchase.

ww.The lender pays the buyer a sum of money: A down payment goes from the buyer to the seller or lender, not the other way; the lender does not pay the buyer anything extra.
ww.The buyer pays nothing, as the lender pa: A down payment means the buyer pays something up front, so saying the buyer pays nothing is the opposite of what a down payment requires.
ww.The buyer pays only the taxes on the sal: Taxes are separate charges; a down payment is part of the purchase price, not just taxes, and it reduces the amount financed.

rw: The loan equals the price minus the down payment: $20,000 - $4,000 = $16,000, which she will repay with interest over time.

ww.$24,000: $24,000 adds the down payment to the price instead of subtracting; paying money up front reduces the loan, so she borrows less than $20,000.
ww.$4,000: $4,000 is the down payment she pays up front, not the amount she borrows; the loan covers the rest of the price.
ww.$20,000: $20,000 is the full price of the car; with a $4,000 down payment she needs to borrow only the remaining $16,000.

rw: Missed or late payments are reported to credit bureaus and hurt scores, since payment history is the largest factor, and repeated misses do the most damage.

ww.Paying all bills on time: Paying all bills on time is the biggest positive factor in credit scores, since payment history carries the most weight, so it raises scores.
ww.Checking your own score free: Checking your own score is a soft inquiry and does not affect it, so doing it for free is safe and does not lower your score.
ww.Keeping your card balances low: Keeping balances low keeps credit utilization down, which is a major scoring factor, so it helps your score rather than lowering it.

rw: An emergency kit and plan prepare you for disasters like storms, fires or outages, with supplies and a plan, so your household stays safe and ready.

ww.To avoid insurance for the whole home: Emergency kits do not replace insurance; they help you survive the first hours or days of a disaster, while insurance helps pay for losses afterward.
ww.To increase spending on luxury goods: An emergency kit holds essentials such as water and flashlights, not luxury goods, and its purpose is safety, not spending.
ww.To store party supplies for events: Party supplies are for celebrations and have no place in an emergency kit, which stores food, water, medicine, batteries and documents.

rw: A $20 warranty on a $30 item costs about two thirds of the price, and replacing the item would cost less than the coverage, so it is usually poor value.

ww.Only if the item is stolen from the shop: Theft of an item from a shop floor is not what a warranty covers; warranties cover defects and breakdowns, so this reason does not justify the cost.
ww.Always, because warranties are free of c: Extended warranties cost money, usually quite a bit, and are not free; the $20 price here is two thirds of the item's $30 cost.
ww.Always, because the item always fails an: Items do not always fail, and most products work fine for years, so paying for a warranty that mostly goes unused is poor value.

rw: Risk is the chance of loss, harm or an unwanted outcome, which is why people use insurance, diversification and safety habits to manage it.

ww.A guaranteed gain on a stock: A guaranteed gain involves no uncertainty, so it is not a risk; risk means a chance of something bad happening.
ww.A tax refund in the spring: A tax refund is money coming back to you, not a chance of loss, so it does not describe risk.
ww.A certain outcome for sure: A certain outcome has no uncertainty, but risk exists only when the result is unknown and a loss is possible.

rw: Diversifying means spreading money across different assets, such as stocks, bonds and funds, so a loss in one does not ruin the whole portfolio.

ww.Borrow more money to invest in stocks: Borrowing to invest in stocks adds leverage and increases risk instead of reducing it, so it is not diversification.
ww.Avoid saving money altogether for good: Avoiding saving does not manage risk; it leaves you with no cushion, while diversification is a method applied to investments you already hold.
ww.Put everything in one asset to watch it: Putting everything in one asset is the opposite of diversification, since one bad event can wipe out your whole investment.

rw: Smoke detectors give early warning of fire, giving you time to escape or stop it, and testing them ensures they work, so they reduce harm.

ww.Leaving candles unattended in a room: Unattended candles are a leading cause of home fires, so leaving them burning increases fire risk rather than reducing it.
ww.Ignoring wiring problems in the home: Ignoring wiring problems can cause electrical fires, so ignoring them raises the risk instead of lowering it.
ww.Overloading outlets with too many plugs: Overloading outlets can overheat wiring and start fires, so it increases the risk of a house fire rather than reducing it.

rw: A rider is an add-on to an insurance policy that extends or changes coverage for a specific item or risk, such as jewelry or flood, usually for extra premium.

ww.A tax on policies that insurers pay to t: Taxes on policies are paid by insurers through premium taxes; a rider is an optional addition to a policy, not a tax.
ww.A refund of premium paid to the holder a: A refund of premium is not a rider; a rider adds coverage to the policy, often at additional cost.
ww.A person who files claims with the insur: A person who files claims is a policyholder or claimant, not a rider, which is a policy provision and not a person.

rw: An umbrella policy adds extra liability coverage above the limits of your home or auto policies, protecting your assets from large lawsuits or judgments.

ww.A discount on premiums for very good dri: Good driver discounts reduce premiums, but an umbrella policy provides extra liability coverage and is not a discount.
ww.Coverage for rain damage only, paid in s: Umbrella policies are not limited to rain; despite the name, they provide extra liability coverage for lawsuits and serious accidents.
ww.Coverage for pets only, not for people o: Umbrella policies protect people and cover liability to others, not just pets, so the coverage is much broader than this suggests.

rw: A worker whose family depends on her paycheck needs disability insurance, which replaces part of her income if illness or injury stops her from working.

ww.A child who is in primary school and has: A young child has no income to replace, so disability insurance is not needed for the child; it protects earnings of working adults.
ww.A person with no income and no dependent: Someone with no income has no earnings to lose, so there is nothing for disability insurance to replace and no dependents rely on it.
ww.A retiree with large savings and a pensi: A retiree with savings and a pension has income that does not depend on working, so disability insurance would add little value.

rw: A scam is a dishonest scheme to steal money or personal information, often by lying, such as fake prizes, phishing messages or fake charities.

ww.A legal agreement signed by two willing: A legal agreement between willing parties is a valid contract, not a scam, because both sides know the terms and agree freely.
ww.A bank statement showing your monthly de: A bank statement is a record of account activity; it shows deposits and withdrawals and is not a dishonest scheme.
ww.A fair trade between two honest parties: A fair trade between honest parties is a normal transaction, the opposite of a scam, which relies on deception.

rw: Real contests do not ask winners to pay fees first, so hanging up is the safe response; you can also report the call to the FTC.

ww.Give your bank details so the prize can: Giving bank details to a stranger lets scammers drain your account or steal your identity, and a real prize never requires them.
ww.Send gift cards to pay the fee for the p: Gift cards are untraceable and a favorite scam payment method, so sending them for a prize fee hands money to criminals.
ww.Pay the fee quickly so that you can clai: Paying a fee to claim a prize is a classic scam sign; legitimate prizes do not require upfront payment, so paying only loses your money.

rw: Trusted sites with secure connections (https and a padlock) protect your payment details, making online purchases safer than on unknown sites.

ww.Share your password with sellers who ask: Sharing your password with a seller gives them access to your accounts, and legitimate sellers never ask for it.
ww.Click every link in emails that you get: Clicking every email link risks phishing and malware, so you should avoid unfamiliar links and go to websites directly.
ww.Use public Wi-Fi at a cafe with no prote: Unprotected public Wi-Fi can let others intercept your data, so shopping on it without a VPN or protection is unsafe.

rw: A W-2 employee is a regular employee whose employer withholds income tax, Social Security and Medicare from each paycheck and reports wages on a W-2 form.

ww.A worker who pays all taxes alone, with: W-2 employees do not pay all taxes alone, since employers withhold income tax and the employer pays half of Social Security and Medicare.
ww.A worker who earns no income from the em: W-2 employees do earn income from the employer; the W-2 form reports those wages, so earning nothing contradicts the term.
ww.A worker paid only in cash, never by che: W-2 employees can be paid by check, direct deposit or cash; the method does not define them, but tax withholding does.

rw: Self-employment tax is about 0.153 x $2,000 = $306 a month, covering both employee and employer shares of Social Security and Medicare.

ww.$3,060: $3,060 is ten times too large; 15.3% of $2,000 is 0.153 x $2,000 = $306, since 15.3% is less than a fifth.
ww.$153: $153 would be 7.65% of $2,000, which is only the employee half; contractors pay both halves, so 15.3% gives $306.
ww.$30.60: $30.60 is only 1.53% of $2,000, a decimal error; 15.3% is ten times that, so the tax is about $306.

rw: A probationary wage is a starting pay rate for a new employee during a trial period, often rising after the employer confirms satisfactory performance.

ww.A tax rate that applies to workers on pr: Probation does not have its own tax rate; the same tax rules apply, and a probationary wage is about the pay rate, not a tax.
ww.A bonus for retirees who leave the firm: A bonus for retirees is a retirement or severance payment, whereas a probationary wage applies to new hires in their trial period.
ww.A permanent top pay level, the highest t: A probationary wage is not a permanent maximum; it is temporary and often rises after the trial period ends.

rw: Benefits like health insurance and employer retirement matches add real value, so a lower paycheck with strong benefits can leave a worker better off overall.

ww.Benefits are always worthless to workers: Benefits such as health insurance and retirement matches have real dollar value, so calling them worthless in the long run is incorrect.
ww.Benefits reduce taxes to zero for most w: Benefits do not reduce taxes to zero; some, like employer health insurance, are tax advantaged, but taxes still apply to your wages.
ww.Pay is the only factor ever worth thinki: Pay is important, but benefits, growth opportunities and stability also matter, so saying pay is the only factor ignores total compensation.

rw: Hourly rate equals pay divided by hours: $48,000 / 2,000 = $24 per hour, which helps compare salaried jobs with hourly jobs.

ww.$240: $240 is ten times too high; $48,000 divided by 2,000 hours is $24, so a decimal slip gives this wrong answer.
ww.$48: $48 mixes up the numbers, perhaps from dropping zeros; $48,000 / 2,000 = $24 per hour, so $48 is double the correct rate.
ww.$2.40: $2.40 is a tenth of the correct rate; $48,000 / 2,000 = $24, so $2.40 is a decimal error.

rw: Frequent short stints can make employers question your commitment and wonder if you will stay, even though some moves have good reasons.

ww.It guarantees promotions, as each new em: Job-hopping does not guarantee promotions; short stints can signal instability, and raises or promotions are not assured at each employer.
ww.It has no effect on how employers see yo: Employers do notice the length of your jobs when reading a résumé, so job-hopping does affect how they view you.
ww.It always raises pay at every new job th: Raises are not guaranteed at every new job; some moves bring bigger pay, but not always, so the claim of always is wrong.

rw: A paid internship is short-term work experience for a wage, often for students, giving practical skills, contacts and a résumé boost.

ww.A type of loan for students at school: A loan is borrowed money that must be repaid; an internship is work experience, and a paid one gives you money.
ww.A tax break for students and interns: An internship is a job experience, not a tax break; students may owe taxes on wages, though some tax credits exist separately.
ww.A permanent contract with a fixed salary: Internships are temporary, often one summer or semester, and rarely carry a permanent contract or fixed salary, so this does not describe one.

rw: Lenders weigh steady income against debts, using ratios like debt-to-income, to judge whether the borrower can make monthly payments over the loan term.

ww.Favorite color of the borrower: A borrower's favorite color has no connection to repayment ability; lenders look at income, debts and credit, not preferences.
ww.Shoe size of the loan applicant: Shoe size has no bearing on repayment ability, and lenders do not consider it when deciding about a loan.
ww.Number of friends the borrower has: The number of friends has no bearing on a person's ability to repay a loan, and lenders do not consider it.

rw: Exempt employees are salaried workers, often in executive or professional roles, who are not entitled to overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

ww.The worker cannot be fired under any cir: Exempt workers can still be fired; the term refers to overtime rules, not job protection, and most employment is at will.
ww.The worker is volunteering for a local c: Volunteering is unpaid work, but exempt refers to salaried employees who are paid and are exempt from overtime rules.
ww.The worker pays no taxes on any of the p: Exempt employees still pay income and payroll taxes on pay; exempt refers to overtime rules, not to taxes.

rw: Store credit cards often carry high APRs, sometimes above 25%, so carrying a balance can erase any discount you earned from signing up.

ww.They are interest-free forever and ever: Store cards are not interest-free forever; interest applies to balances you carry, and deferred interest promotions can charge back interest if not paid in time.
ww.They improve your credit automatically: Store cards do not improve credit automatically; they can hurt your score through hard inquiries, high utilization or missed payments.
ww.They always charge no fees of any kind: Store cards can charge late fees and other fees, and some have annual fees, so saying they never have fees is false.

rw: Paying $450 cash is cheaper than the $500 price on the plan, saving $50, even though the plan has 0% interest.

ww.Neither costs: Both options cost money, since one is $450 and the other is $500, so saying neither costs is not true.
ww.$500 on plan: The 12-month plan totals $500 even with 0% interest, which is $50 more than the $450 cash price, so it is the more expensive choice.
ww.They are even: The totals are $450 versus $500, a $50 difference, so they are not even; paying cash costs less.

rw: A gift card scam is when someone demands payment with gift cards, because they are hard to trace and recover, which is a common fraud tactic.

ww.A store discount given to loyal customer: A loyalty discount is a legitimate store reward; a gift card scam is a fraud in which a scammer demands payment in gift cards.
ww.A required payment method for bills, acc: Utilities and legitimate businesses do not demand payment by gift card; that demand is a scam sign, so it is not a required method.
ww.A tax refund that is paid out to the buy: Tax refunds are not paid in gift cards; the IRS pays by direct deposit or check, so this is not a description of the scam.

rw: Being frugal means using money carefully and avoiding waste, by comparing prices, buying what you need and cutting unnecessary costs.

ww.Buying luxury items only, nothing else: Buying only luxury items is wasteful spending, the opposite of frugal, which means using resources carefully and avoiding waste.
ww.Avoiding all spending for a month: Avoiding all spending for a month is extreme and not practical, since you still need food and housing; frugal means careful spending, not none.
ww.Spending with no thought on any item: Spending with no thought is the opposite of frugal, which means thinking carefully about each purchase and avoiding waste.

rw: Weekly waste is 0.15 x $200 = $30, and over 52 weeks that is $30 x 52 = $1,560 of wasted food per year.

ww.$15,600: $15,600 is ten times too large; 15% of $200 is $30 a week, and $30 x 52 weeks is $1,560.
ww.$30: $30 is only the weekly waste (0.15 x $200); the question asks for a year, so multiply by 52 weeks.
ww.$156: $156 is a tenth of the correct amount; $30 per week times 52 weeks equals $1,560, so this is a decimal error.

rw: Paying yourself first means moving money to savings right when you get paid, before other spending, so saving becomes automatic and consistent.

ww.Skip savings and spend all of your pay f: Skipping savings and spending everything first is the opposite of paying yourself first, which puts savings ahead of spending.
ww.Spend before saving anything at all from: Spending before saving is exactly what paying yourself first avoids; the idea is to save first and spend what is left.
ww.Pay bills last, after all of your spendi: Paying bills last is not the idea; paying yourself first means setting aside savings, then paying bills with the remainder.

rw: Comparison sites list prices from many sellers so you can find the lowest price, including shipping, before you buy.

ww.Hiding fees from the shoppers who visit: Price comparison sites show prices openly, so they help shoppers see total costs rather than hiding them.
ww.Delaying delivery of an order for a day: Comparison sites do not delay deliveries; they only show prices and links, and the seller handles delivery.
ww.Raising prices for the buyers who visit: Comparison sites help shoppers find lower prices, so raising prices is the opposite of their usefulness.

rw: A well-made jacket that lasts many seasons has a low cost per use because the price is spread over many wears.

ww.A trendy jacket that is worn only once: A trendy jacket worn only once has a very high cost per use and quickly goes out of style, so it is poor value.
ww.No jacket at all, just a thin summer shi: No jacket leaves you unprotected from cold weather, and a thin shirt is not a substitute, so it does not meet the goal.
ww.The cheapest jacket that tears quickly: The cheapest jacket that tears quickly must be replaced often, so the total cost over time is higher, and the cost per use is high.

rw: A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered, and rational decisions should ignore it and look only at future costs and benefits.

ww.A tax on boats that sink in the deep sea: Boat taxes are unrelated; a sunk cost is any money already spent that cannot be recovered, and it should not drive future decisions.
ww.Money you will spend later on other thin: Money you will spend later is a future cost, which can still be avoided, unlike a sunk cost that has already been paid.
ww.Money you can still get back if canceled: If money can still be recovered, such as through a refund, it is not a sunk cost, which is spent and gone for good.
